name: Salt (sodium chloride) and lithium
short: People taking lithium: low salt can raise lithium to toxic levels; changes in salt intake can change lithium levels. A review tells prescribers to counteract such changes or adjust the lithium dose.
text: This is a harm-focused entry centred on the interaction between salt intake and the psychiatric medicine lithium, with related cautions about sodium restriction from the same sources; it does not cover the wider health effects of salt. Two reviews state that low sodium intake reduces the kidneys' clearance of lithium and that sodium restriction can enhance reabsorption of lithium, leading to toxic blood concentrations; one also lists dehydration, diuretics, blood-pressure drugs and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs as reducing lithium clearance, and the other states that sodium restriction together with ACE inhibitors, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or immunosuppressive drugs can precipitate acute kidney failure. One review addresses clinicians, stating that they should counteract conditions under which lithium clearance changes and, if that is not possible, adjust the lithium dose to the clearance. In a kidney-physiology study in 103 healthy people at varying sodium intakes, including marked restriction, which examined lithium clearance as a research index of filtrate delivery from the kidney's proximal tubules, lithium clearance fell gradually as fractional sodium excretion fell. A review of lithium poisoning, whose abstract does not mention salt intake, describes lithium as having a narrow therapeutic index; chronic poisoning, the most common type, results from intake exceeding elimination, most often because of impaired kidney function from volume depletion, and can range from raised blood levels without symptoms to confusion, unsteadiness or seizures, with persistent neurological damage described, although the death rate is low. In a randomised trial in 60 people with bipolar I disorder taking lithium, whose blood lithium, sodium and potassium were measured at 4, 8 and 12 weeks, fewer patients given 1 g of sodium chloride a day (and told to limit extra table salt to 1 g a day) had fluctuations in blood lithium, defined as a level below 0.6 or above 0.8 mEq/L, than those advised to add no salt at the table (26.7% versus 63.3%); blood lithium also differed significantly between the groups at 8 and 12 weeks, but the abstract does not give the direction of that difference, and there were no significant changes in blood sodium, potassium, kidney function or blood pressure; the authors concluded that this add-on sodium chloride may reduce fluctuations in blood lithium during maintenance lithium treatment. A case report on lithium in pregnancy recommended careful monitoring of side effects, dose and blood lithium levels if salt restriction or diuretics are needed. The evidence therefore comes from reviews, one physiological study, one small randomised trial and one case report.
